newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian premier says 1997 will see growth.
newsitem.headline: Russian premier says 1997 will see growth.

text.p: Viktor Chernomyrdin, marking four years as prime minister, predicted on Saturday that Russia would return to long-awaited economic growth in 1997 after several years of decline.

"1997 is the breakthrough year, the real thing. The breakthough is built into the law. We have envisaged two percent growth of GDP (gross domestic product)...It's not just Chernomyrdin's wishful thinking," he said in a television interview.

A year ago, Russian officials expressed optimism that 1996 would see the first post-reform growth in GDP. But official statistics issued on Saturday showed a six percent drop in GDP over the first 11 months against the same 1995 period.
"The next task is to go through with it," Chernomyrdin said, referring to the 1997 budget draft, which is due to be considered by the lower house of parliament on Sunday.

Opposition deputies put off debate on the budget when they first considered it on December 6, but top parliamentary officials said on Saturday they were likely to approve it on Sunday, although there was set to be a fierce debate.
Chernomyrdin said that it would be hard to stick to the budget, which envisages a deficit no larger than 3.5 percent of GDP, but that it was crucial to pull Russia out of economic crisis.
"It's difficult but in any case it will radically change the situation in the country," he said in the interview broadcast on Russian Public Television.
An economic programme to the year 2000 would be presented to parliament by December 25 which will envisage up to six percent growth in output by then, Chernomyrdin said.
President Boris Yeltsin is due to return to the Kremlin on that day after almost six months of heart problems and surgery.
The report is expected to be one of several he has commissioned on the government's work during his illness, which led to a multiple heart bypass operation in November.
Summing up his time at the helm of the Russian government Chernomyrdin conceeded that it had been focused on damage limitation. "I think that a lot was done to keep Russia from destruction," he said.
